clinicalPearls: Defined by rearrangement of the NUTM1 gene, most often fused to BRD4 (less commonly BRD3 or NSD3), producing an oncogenic fusion protein that blocks squamous differentiation
Arises predominantly in midline structures such as the mediastinum, thymus, lung and head and neck, though non-midline sites are increasingly recognised
Typically affects children, adolescents and younger adults, but can occur at any age and shows no strong sex predilection
Histology shows a monotonous poorly differentiated carcinoma with abrupt (rather than gradual) foci of squamous keratinisation
Diagnosis is confirmed by the monoclonal NUT immunohistochemical antibody, which gives a characteristic speckled nuclear staining pattern in the majority of cases
Should be considered in any young patient with an aggressive undifferentiated or poorly differentiated midline carcinoma of unknown primary
Often initially misdiagnosed as another poorly differentiated squamous carcinoma, thymic carcinoma, Ewing sarcoma or germ cell tumour before molecular testing
reference.pathophysiology: NUT carcinoma is driven by a balanced rearrangement of the NUTM1 gene, most commonly generating a BRD4-NUT fusion in which a bromodomain protein is joined to nuclear protein in testis. The fusion protein sequesters histone-modifying machinery and drives aberrant chromatin acetylation across large genomic regions, locking cells in a proliferative, undifferentiated state and preventing terminal squamous maturation. This single genetic event is sufficient to produce a highly aggressive epithelial malignancy, and the resulting dependence on chromatin readers and acetylation underpins interest in bromodomain and histone-deacetylase directed therapies.
additionalDifferentials: Poorly differentiated or basaloid squamous cell carcinoma
Thymic carcinoma and other mediastinal carcinomas
Ewing sarcoma and other small round blue cell tumours
Germ cell tumour, particularly in mediastinal disease
additionalInvestigations: NUT immunohistochemistry showing speckled nuclear positivity as the principal screening test
Molecular confirmation of NUTM1 rearrangement by FISH break-apart probe or next-generation sequencing
Broad immunohistochemical panel including squamous, epithelial, germ cell and haematolymphoid markers to exclude mimics
Cross-sectional imaging of chest, abdomen and pelvis to define the primary site and stage disease
Biopsy with adequate tissue for ancillary molecular studies given the undifferentiated appearance
Assessment for distant metastases, which are frequently present at diagnosis
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging midline mass in a child, adolescent or young adult
Airway compromise or superior vena cava obstruction from a bulky mediastinal or thoracic tumour
Widespread metastatic disease at presentation, often to bone and lung
Aggressive clinical course with rapid progression despite conventional therapy
reference.prognosis: NUT carcinoma is one of the most aggressive human solid tumours, with rapid local progression, early metastasis and generally short survival despite multimodality treatment; long-term survival is uncommon, although outcomes may be marginally better for non-thoracic primaries amenable to complete surgical resection combined with radiotherapy, and targeted agents remain investigational.
pitfalls: Mistaking the tumour for ordinary poorly differentiated squamous carcinoma and not requesting NUT testing
Overlooking the diagnosis in older adults or non-midline sites where it is less expected
Interpreting focal keratinisation as evidence of a more differentiated, less aggressive carcinoma
Failing to preserve tissue for molecular confirmation when the initial impression is a small round cell tumour
Attributing weak or patchy NUT staining to a negative result without confirmatory molecular studies
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Thoracic Tumours
WHO Classification of Tumours: Head and Neck Tumours
management: For localized resectable disease, pursue complete surgical resection where feasible, generally combined with radiotherapy for local control.
For locally advanced unresectable disease, definitive radiotherapy is a reasonable option for local control given resistance to conventional chemotherapy.

For metastatic disease, conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy has not been shown to improve outcomes and should not be relied on; prioritize clinical trial enrollment and early palliative and supportive care.
Bromodomain (BET) inhibitors are an investigational epigenetic class aimed at restoring differentiation gene expression, available mainly through clinical trials.
Histone deacetylase inhibitors are another investigational class exploiting the same fusion biology and should be considered trial-based rather than established therapy.
Because effective systemic options outside trials are lacking, refer early to a center with access to experimental therapy protocols once diagnosis is confirmed.
Radiotherapy, whether definitive or adjuvant after resection, should be part of local management whenever feasible.
Multidisciplinary planning involving surgery, radiation oncology, medical oncology, and pathology is warranted given the disease's rarity and aggressiveness.
Maintain close surveillance for rapid local recurrence and distant metastasis given the aggressive course and short expected survival.
Build reassessment for distant metastatic disease into follow-up, since metastases are frequently present at diagnosis.
Refer any suspected case promptly to a center experienced with this diagnosis for confirmatory testing and clinical trial access.
Involve specialized multidisciplinary oncology teams and palliative and supportive care early, rather than waiting until conventional therapy has failed.
